section_summaries.epidemiology: Campylobacter is the most common bacterial zoonotic disease globally, with warm-blooded animals (e.g., poultry, pigs, cattle, sheep, dogs, cats, wild animals) serving as main reservoirs. Transmission to humans occurs through handling and consumption of animal food products, environmental contact, and direct animal contact, with 50% to 70% of human infection strains attributed to poultry. Targeted interventions in countries like Iceland and New Zealand have significantly reduced incidence. Surface water and outbreaks are also important pathways of transmission. Seasonal fluctuations are observed in the summer and early autumn in the United States and Europe. The increasing use of culture-independent diagnostic tests (CIDTs) has complicated surveillance data interpretation, though the incidence of culture-confirmed infections decreased between 1996 and 2016 in the United States and significantly in New Zealand. Surveillance of enteric infections is common in high-income countries but rare in low-income settings, where Campylobacter isolation rates in children with diarrhea range from 5% to 20%. Adults in low-income countries are often asymptomatic due to acquired immunity. Travelers, especially to Asia, Africa, and Central and South America, are a specific population at risk. Post-infectious complications like Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), Reactive Arthritis (ReA), and Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) contribute significantly to the global disease burden.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Campylobacter infection can lead to Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) by inducing a complement-mediated immune response targeting specific glycan structures on the surface lipooligosaccharides of certain C. jejuni strains that cross-react with human nerve gangliosides. In breastfed infants, protection against Campylobacter is mediated by acquired and innate defense factors in human milk, including antibodies, oligosaccharides, and their glycol-conjugates. Human milk oligosaccharides have been shown experimentally to inhibit disease pathogenesis and reduce disease severity in vitro and in mouse models of C. jejuni infection.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: A low infective dose of C. jejuni (360 CFU/mL) can cause diarrhea in healthy volunteers, with symptoms typically appearing 1 to 3 days after ingestion. Common symptoms include diarrhea, malaise, fever, and abdominal pain. The clinical spectrum ranges from watery diarrhea to dysentery and may include mesenteric adenitis. In high-income countries, C. jejuni enteritis can be severe in children and adults, often presenting with bloody diarrhea. In low-income countries, it is usually milder and more often watery. The incidence and duration of illness tend to decrease with age, and asymptomatic infections or intermittent carriership are frequently observed in adults. Gastroenteritis is usually self-limited, lasting up to 7 days, though a minority of patients experience persistent abdominal symptoms. Bacteremia is more frequent in younger and elderly patients. Untreated individuals may excrete Campylobacter for 2 to 3 weeks. Rare extra-intestinal sequelae include bacteremia, meningitis, endocarditis, cellulitis, peritonitis, and brain abscesses. Post-infectious complications such as IBS, ReA, and GBS usually present within 3 months of infection, with GBS often within 3 weeks. GBS is an acute, immune-mediated flaccid paralysis where C. jejuni is the most common antecedent infection worldwide, with symptoms occurring 1 to 3 weeks after enteritis. IBS manifests as persistent abdominal discomfort, bloating, and diarrhea alternating with constipation. ReA is an inflammatory arthritis, typically developing within 3 months after a gastrointestinal infection, characterized by sterile joint inflammation, absence of rheumatoid factors, and frequent extra-articular symptoms, with a predilection for the lower extremities.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Stool samples for diagnosis should be placed in transport medium (e.g., Cary-Blair) and kept cool if a delay is anticipated. Campylobacter is difficult to isolate, grow, and identify, with C. jejuni being the only species routinely identified by phenotypic markers. C. jejuni and C. coli require specialized, enriched, selective media (blood-containing or charcoal-containing with antibiotic mixtures) incubated at 37°C or, preferably, 42°C under microaerobic conditions. Passive filtration is an alternative culture-based method for resource-limited settings. Culture-independent diagnostic tests (CIDTs), including DNA-based methods and enzyme immunoassays, have increased the sensitivity of laboratory confirmation, though stool antigen CIDT sensitivity and specificity can be variable. PCR-based assays are increasingly replacing culture in high-income countries and are approved by the FDA. The clinical relevance of non-C. jejuni or non-C. coli species remains unclear. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) has replaced serotyping for reservoir and pathway attribution, and whole genome sequencing is increasingly used for clinical and epidemiologic studies.
section_summaries.treatment: Campylobacter enteritis is often a self-limited infection that does not require antimicrobial treatment. The most important intervention is supportive and rehydration therapy. Antimicrobial treatment is indicated for severe, persistent, or relapsing infections (e.g., bacteremia) and in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV, agammaglobulinemia, pregnant women). Macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) and fluoroquinolones are widely advocated as first-line treatments, though fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnant women. Resistance of C. jejuni to fluoroquinolones is a major global problem, particularly in Southeast Asia, largely attributed to widespread use in animal husbandry. Macrolide resistance is currently low but slowly rising. For immunocompromised patients with bacteremia, treatment should be guided by susceptibility tests, and regimens may include carbapenem antibiotics (e.g., meropenem and imipenem) combined with aminoglycosides.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention of Campylobacter infections requires a multi-tiered approach due to its complex epidemiology. Targeted interventions at the food chain level have shown to reduce human incidence, for example, by 74% in Iceland and 54% in New Zealand. At the consumer level, appropriate precautions during handling and preparation of animal foods are crucial to reduce cross-contamination, including adequate cooking of raw meat and poultry, thorough hand washing after handling raw foods, and proper cleaning of chopping boards. Development of vaccines for Campylobacter is challenging due to antigenic diversity, the lack of small animal models, and cross-reactive complement-mediated immune responses (e.g., leading to GBS) that preclude whole-cell vaccine approaches. Recent vaccine studies have focused on recombinant protein subunit antigens and capsular polysaccharide-conjugate vaccines, but no commercially available vaccine exists for humans yet.
